segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some of them disobey the word, they may be won over without a word through their wives' conduct,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: when they have observed your pure and reverent conduct.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Your adornment should not be the outward one of braiding hair, wearing gold jewelry, or putting on clothes,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but the hidden person of the heart, with what is imperishable: a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great value in God's sight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is how the holy women of the past who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, being subject to their own husbands,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. You have become her children, doing good and not fearing anything that terrifies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Husbands, in the same way, live with your wives with understanding, showing honor to the woman as to a weaker vessel, since they are also fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finally, all of you: be of one mind, sympathetic, loving toward one another as brothers and sisters, tender-hearted, humble in mind,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not repaying evil for evil or insult for insult, but on the contrary blessing, because you were called to this, so that you might inherit a blessing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “whoever wants to love life and see good days must keep the tongue from evil and the lips from speaking deceit,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: must turn away from evil and do good, must seek peace and pursue it;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: for the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous and his ears are open to their plea, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And who is going to harm you if you become zealous for what is good?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But even if you should suffer because of righteousness, you are blessed. Have no fear of them, and do not be troubled,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always ready to give a defense to anyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: yet with gentleness and reverence, keeping a good conscience, so that when you are slandered, those who disparage your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is better to suffer for doing good, if the will of God should so will, than for doing evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring you to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in which he also went and made proclamation to the spirits in prison,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who had once disobeyed, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah while an ark was being built, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were saved through water.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Baptism, the counterpart of this, now saves you too—not as the removal of dirt from the flesh but as the pledge of a good conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who has gone into heaven and is at God's right hand, with angels and authorities and powers made subject to him.

notes.note: The Greek says the conduct is ‘in fear’. Most interpreters take this as reverence toward God, in line with the letter's usage elsewhere, and that reading is followed here and in verse 16. Some take it as respect toward the husband.

The Greek has only ‘putting on of garments’, with no word for ‘fine’ or ‘expensive’. Many translations add the adjective because the point is plainly about display, not about dressing at all. The plain wording is kept here, and the context supplies the sense.

The traditional ‘meek’ now suggests weakness, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone who is not self-assertive or harsh. ‘Gentle’ or ‘humble’ is the usual modern rendering, and the related noun in verse 16 is translated ‘gentleness’.

The reference is to Genesis 18:12, where Sarah speaks of Abraham as ‘my lord’. The word was an ordinary term of respect for a husband or master, much like ‘sir’, and does not imply divinity here. The closing words about fearing nothing that terrifies echo Proverbs 3:25.

‘Vessel’ was a common image for a human being as a body or creature, and the comparative ‘weaker’ implies that the husband is a vessel too. Most interpreters take the weakness as physical strength or social vulnerability, not moral or intellectual inferiority; the verse goes on to call wives fellow heirs. Some translations paraphrase as ‘weaker partner’ or ‘weaker sex’.

Verses 10–12 quote Psalm 34:12–16 in a form close to the Greek Septuagint. Greek has a single word-family where English has two: ‘righteous’ and ‘just’, ‘righteousness’ and ‘justice’. The same family appears in ‘righteousness’ (verse 14) and ‘the righteous for the unrighteous’ (verse 18).

notes.traditional: be not afraid of their terror
notes.note: Literally ‘do not fear their fear’, borrowed from Isaiah 8:12, where it means ‘do not fear what they fear’. In this letter's setting most interpreters take it as ‘do not be afraid of them’, meaning the opponents, and that is followed here. The Isaiah sense remains possible, and some translations adopt it.

notes.phrase: honor Christ the Lord as holy
notes.note: The wording continues the allusion to Isaiah 8:13, ‘regard the Lord as holy’, and applies it to Christ. Later manuscripts read ‘the Lord God’, which the King James Version follows; the earliest witnesses read ‘Christ’. The phrase can also be construed as ‘honor Christ as Lord’.

Many early manuscripts read ‘died’ in place of ‘suffered’, and some read ‘bring us’ in place of ‘bring you’. ‘Suffered’ fits the letter's running theme and is the reading of the Greek text translated here, but the choice is disputed.

‘Flesh’ and ‘spirit’ are set in parallel with no preposition in Greek. Most scholars take them as two spheres or modes of existence: Christ was put to death as a mortal human and made alive in the realm of the spirit, that is, in resurrection. Others read the second as ‘by the Spirit’, naming the Holy Spirit as agent.

This is one of the most disputed verses in the New Testament. Many modern scholars identify the spirits as the rebellious angelic beings of Genesis 6, whom Jewish tradition such as 1 Enoch describes as imprisoned, with the risen Christ announcing his victory to them. Others take them as the human dead of Noah's generation, or hold that Christ preached through Noah to people then living. The verb means only ‘announce as a herald’ and does not state what was proclaimed.

notes.phrase: the pledge of a good conscience toward God
notes.traditional: the answer of a good conscience toward God
notes.note: The Greek noun is rare, and its meaning here is disputed. In contracts of the period it is used for a formal undertaking, which supports ‘pledge’. The related verb means ‘ask’, which supports ‘an appeal to God for a good conscience’, the choice of several major translations. Either way, the contrast is between washing the outside and an inward commitment directed to God.

candidates.rendering: be subject to / made subject to
candidates.reason: Recurs across the household codes, Romans 13 and Christological passages; translators vary between ‘submit’, ‘be subject’ and ‘be subordinate’, and readers will notice the variation.
Ranges from the physical body to mortal human existence to Paul's ethical sense; it needs a policy on when to keep ‘flesh’ and when to paraphrase.
Means ‘life’, ‘self’, ‘person’ or ‘soul’ depending on context; the traditional ‘soul’ often misleads, and a consistent policy is needed across books.
A key term in 1 Peter and found in Paul, Hebrews and James; it is rendered ‘conduct’, ‘way of life’ or ‘behaviour’ and should be uniform.
‘Preach’ now suggests sermons, while the Greek means to announce as a herald; a single decision on ‘proclaim’ versus ‘preach’ is needed for the whole New Testament.
